name: Ancient Egyptian religion
areas: the gods of Egypt's towns and of its kings
the last temples, as Egypt became Christian
priests of Isis served the Nubian peoples beyond the border
Amun of Napata and the gods of Egypt, honoured by the kings of Kush and Meroë
Egyptian temples and garrisons under the New Kingdom
Isis and Serapis in the Greek world
temples of Isis at Rome and Pompeii
the cult of Isis across the Roman Empire
routes: The New Kingdom carries Amun's worship into Nubia
Isis and Serapis cross the Mediterranean
marks: Nekhen (Hierakonpolis), an early centre of the falcon god Horus, where the Narmer Palette, a record of the first kings, was found.
The Great Pyramid was built as the tomb of the king Khufu around 2560 BCE.
The Pyramid Texts, Egypt's oldest religious writings, were carved in the pyramid of Unas around 2350 BCE.
The great temple of Amun-Ra at Thebes, built and enlarged over two thousand years from the Middle Kingdom on.
The cult centre of Osiris, god of the dead, where pilgrims gathered for his festival.
The "Pure Mountain" of Amun in Nubia, honoured by the kings of the New Kingdom and later by the kings of Kush.
Akhenaten founded his new capital here for the Aten, the sun disc, around 1350 BCE.
The temple of Isis at Pompeii, rebuilt after the earthquake of 62 and buried by Vesuvius in 79.
The Serapeum of Alexandria was destroyed in 391, after Theodosius banned pagan sacrifice.
The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved here in 394; officials of Justinian closed the temple of Isis around 537.
notes: Egypt is united under the first kings, who rule as the god Horus on earth; the gods of its towns join a shared religion.
The Old Kingdom: kings build the pyramids of Giza (around 2560 BCE), and the sun god Ra rises to supremacy.
The Pyramid Texts, Egypt's oldest religious writings, are carved in the pyramid of Unas (around 2350 BCE).
After the Old Kingdom falls, the hope of life after death with Osiris spreads beyond the king to all who can afford a proper burial.
The Middle Kingdom builds the first temples at Karnak for Amun of Thebes; Egypt's fortresses and temples reach Lower Nubia.
The New Kingdom: Amun-Ra of Thebes becomes the king of the gods, Egypt's temples spread into Nubia and Canaan, and the Book of the Dead guides the dead.
Akhenaten raises the Aten, the sun disc, above all other gods and founds Amarna; after his death the old gods are restored.
Ramesses II builds Abu Simbel and enlarges Karnak and Luxor.
Kings of Kush, devotees of Amun, rule Egypt as the 25th Dynasty.
The Persians conquer Egypt (525 BCE); the temples keep their rites under foreign kings.
The Ptolemies, Macedonian kings of Egypt, build temples in the old style and promote the god Serapis; Isis is worshipped across the Greek world.
Rome annexes Egypt (30 BCE); its emperors are shown on temple walls as pharaohs, and Isis has temples from Rome to Britain.
Christianity spreads along the Nile, and the temples lose their income and their priests.
Theodosius bans pagan sacrifice; the Serapeum of Alexandria is destroyed (391), and the last known hieroglyphic inscription is carved at Philae (394).
Only on the southern frontier, at Philae, do priests still serve Isis, honoured by the Nubian peoples beyond the border.
Officials of Justinian close the temple of Isis at Philae (around 537), the end of Egypt's ancient religion.
src: Erik Hornung, Conceptions of God in Ancient Egypt (1982)
Richard H. Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
John Baines and Jaromír Málek, Atlas of Ancient Egypt (1980)
David Frankfurter, Religion in Roman Egypt (1998)
